forms.why_en: Moi is the everyday spoken hello. Books and formal texts write hei.
Minä with -n: minun pitää means I have to. Speech shortens it to mun.

forms.form_name_en: nominative singular, with the possessive ending for my
forms.why_en: Adds -ni for 'my': suihku becomes suihkuni. Speech just says mun suihku.
Ei on its own answers 'no'. People say it the same way.
After ei the verb drops its ending: toimia becomes toimi.
Okei is the everyday spoken OK. Books write selvä, which means clear.

forms.form_name_en: present tense, 3rd person singular, with the question ending -ko/-kö
forms.why_en: Tulla takes -ee for 'it' and -ko to ask: tuleeko. Speech says tuleeks.
The elative singular of se 'it': siitä, 'out of it'. Speech drops the last ä: siit.
This is the dictionary form. People say it the same way.
The partitive singular is used for some water: vesi becomes vettä, the si turning to tt.
Speech says vaan. Books write vain.

Mikä with -hin for 'to': mihin, where to.

Adds -sta for 'from': kahdeksan becomes kahdeksasta. Speech says kaheksast.
The illative singular gives 'until' with a clock time: neljä becomes neljään.
Voida, can, with -n for 'I': voin.
